Animated GIF rendering is handled by your browser and to date there's not a single browser that supports 60FPS GIF animation. What you're seeing is going to depend on your browser. It's going to range from 50FPS (Chrome, Opera, FireFox) to as low as 16FPS (Safari, IE) depending on your browser and its configuration. Like somebody already linked here is an app that ought be able to universally show the difference (definitely play with the motion blur options on the top to understand the real differences). Another idea if you want just a linkable media file would be to use a .webm file.

edit Elaborating on this. Some folks might think "Well 50 is really close to 60." In reality a 60FPS image actually has 50% more frames than 50FPS relative to the difference between 30FPS, eg - an additional 30 vs an additional 20 FPS. It's a major difference.
I find it interesting (funny) that the worst performing browsers are the ones that are installed by default and made by OS companies.

But you think CRTs were still better for some reason?

You know the obsession with gray-to-gray response times? Nonexistent in CRTs.

Yes, they are bulky, heavy, not perfectly flat, and use more power. But they exhibit no ghosting, blur, clouding, or other weird artifacts that reviewers look for in LCD reviews.

Dynamic contrast ratios can easily be 15,000 to 1 whereas an LCD might have 500:1 (1,000:1 with variable backlighting tricks). Black is truly black (0.01 cd/m2 vs 0.25 for lcd).

Don't get me wrong, I would much prefer an LCD for convenience, plus, a CRT is like a big electron gun that sits a few feet from your head. You really don't want to be exposed to that sort of radiation given how much time we spend in front of computers these days. But we have not matched the quality of CRTs with LCDs and probably never will. OLED looks promising but it's still got a ways to go before it becomes a common option.

Usually, there is a huge difference in input response as well. Most games run in a big, linear loop. First they poll for input, then they calculate movement or AI, then they draw the graphics and display them. So if a game is completing that loop 60 times a second vs 30, then it has twice as often to figure out where you've moved the mouse or what keys you've hit.
